Boundary regularity and conic decomposition

Written and self-checked by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra, October 2026. Public domain (CC0).

A singular covector can be read at one point on the boundary of a complex tube. This lesson proves the exact correspondence: Fourier regularity in the direction is equivalent to derivative bounds near the boundary point . The correspondence works for smooth, analytic and all the derivative-growth classes considered here. It then gives a decomposition subordinate to any finite closed conic cover, together with the precise ambiguity on cone intersections.

The main inputs are Derivative growth and finite-order localization, Lemmas 1 and 5 and Proposition 3; Cones and derivative-growth wavefronts, the definition and Theorems 3, 5–7; Holomorphic decompositions of tempered distributions, Lemma 1, Theorems 3–5 and Proposition 6; and Continuing the spherical kernel, Corollary 8 and its uniform analytic remainder. The Schwartz and Fourier foundation, F1–F5, supplies Fourier inversion and pairings. Integral Taylor remainders are proved in When a kernel is smooth, and polydisk Cauchy bounds in Holomorphic boundaries in convex cones. The integration foundation, Sections 15–16, supplies the finite measures and limiting operations below.

Proof. If , the earlier analytic angular bound excludes from , hence from by the proved class comparison.

Suppose instead that is smooth at , where . Take a smaller ball inside the ball of all-order bounds. Its intersection with is convex. The bound on derivatives of order , together with the Cauchy–Riemann equations, makes Lipschitz there. Its values therefore extend uniquely and continuously to the closure: interior approximations are Cauchy by that bound, and any two approximations have the same limit. Each derivative retains its original bound. For real near and in a small closed spherical cap about , denote the extended value of by .

At height , , apply the fundamental theorem along a small real coordinate segment. Passing to uniformly on that segment gives the same identity with the extended first derivative. Repeating for every proves that is smooth with these derivatives and their common bounds. Uniform convergence on compact real sets identifies this function with the distributional boundary there. Choose an open cap about whose closure is such a cap. Split . Dominated convergence against the finite total variation measure makes the first contribution smooth near . The second measure's support avoids , so its contribution is analytically regular in the direction .

For completeness, the smooth sum rule needed in this last step follows directly from the Fourier cutoff argument already used in the conic lesson. On the cone of rapid decay, distribute any output weight using and take both decay exponents greater than the output exponent plus . Examples and exercises with complete solutions

Exercise 1 — the sign and the normalization (foundation). In dimension one take , . Compute the two Fourier multipliers in (21). Apply them to the constant function.

Solution. Here , and each sphere point has mass one. Positive covectors use the bottom boundary. Consequently

These multipliers are smooth with polynomially bounded derivatives, as already proved for the boundary multipliers. Their sum is one. The transform of is , so each gives the constant . The total is one, even though the zero frequency belongs to neither cone: the cones constrain singular directions, not the support of these multipliers.

Exercise 2 — conic pieces are not projections (intermediate). For the preceding one-dimensional splitting, prove that . Show nevertheless that every has wavefront in , for every regularity choice , and interpret the conclusion.

Solution. Apply twice to : the answers are and . Thus idempotence fails. Since , and . Theorem 4 twice places each output wavefront in both cones. Their intersection is empty, so the outputs have empty analytic wavefront. The projection theorem for in the conic lesson makes them real analytic everywhere. This assertion does not say that they vanish or are entire functions.

Exercise 3 — changing the ordering (intermediate). Order the same finite closed cover in two different ways and form the decompositions of Theorem 4. Prove that the resulting difference in each term is accounted for by intersections, even if the cone boundaries have positive surface measure. If all intersections involving are empty, what can change in its component?

Solution. Relabel the second decomposition by the original cone names. Both decompositions satisfy (20). Theorem 5 supplies antisymmetric differences obeying (22); its proof uses Borel restrictions and support inclusions, with no null-boundary assumption. If every for is empty, apply the theorem for . Every is real analytic by the projection theorem, and ; hence the component changes at most by a real analytic function. For this particular first-membership construction an entirely disjoint cone actually has the same assigned sphere piece in either ordering, so its component does not change at all. The analytic conclusion also holds for arbitrary decompositions satisfying the same analytic wavefront bounds.

Exercise 4 — a point source has every direction (advanced). Prove directly that , and deduce the corresponding statement for every . Describe what this says about the boundary regularity of , the tube function of .

Solution. At a nonzero base point choose a cutoff supported away from the origin; its product with is zero, giving witnesses in every class. At the origin any cutoff equal to one nearby leaves unchanged. Its Fourier transform is the constant one, which is not rapidly decreasing along any nonempty frequency cone. This proves the smooth assertion. The class sandwich , together with the zero witnesses away from the origin, gives the same exact set for every . By Theorem 3 the kernel is not smooth at any , and is not -regular there for any admissible . At with , it extends holomorphically to a full neighborhood. This latter statement also follows from the off-support theorem applied to and a small ball about .

Exercise 5 — local distributions and a canonical regularity test (advanced). Let , where is any open subset of , and let . Choose equal to one near , extend by zero, and form its tube function. Show that Theorem 3 tests the wavefront of at , independently of .

Solution. The compact distribution is tempered by its finite-order bound. Near it agrees with . The definition of -regularity is unchanged on restricting to a smaller neighborhood: a witness equal to one distribution there is a witness for the other. Compact supports can be placed inside that neighborhood using the controlled localization Theorem 3 of the conic lesson. This proves the local equality of their -wavefront sets. The smooth version follows from the cutoff transfer (16). Thus Theorem 3 applies to the original local wavefront. If are two choices, their compactly supported difference vanishes on a fixed neighborhood of . Its tube function extends holomorphically near every , by the off-support theorem. Adding this function preserves (4), smooth bounds, and existence of holomorphic extension in both directions, after shrinking the neighborhood. This also proves independence directly at the boundary. No global extension of and no identification of with Euclidean space is required.
